title: Human Gingival Crevicular Fluid Reveals the Occurrence of Ferroptosis During Clinical Progression of Periodontitis
projectDescription: Thirteen healthy men diagnosed with periodontitis were enrolled. Progression of periodontitis was monitored by clinical attachment level (CAL) changes at the site level over twelve weeks via weekly clinical evaluations and gingival crevicular fluid (GCF) samples were collected using cellulose strips for subsequent mass spectrometry analysis. Progression group (PG) included 18 GCF samples matching sites with disease progression (CAL ≥ 2 mm), while the non-Progression group (NP) included 18 GCF samples from stable sites (No CAL changes) matched in the same patients.  Clinical metrics, HPRLC-MS/MS, in silico methods, and bioinformatics tools, were employed to analyze the proteome of GCF, revealing the significant occurrence of ferroptosis during clinical progression of periodontitis.
sampleProcessingProtocol: The proteins were eluted from Periopaper strips. Briefly, the paper strips were kept at 4°C overnight in 150 μl of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) with a 2x protease inhibitor cocktail. The samples were then centrifuged at 400 G for 4 minutes at 4°C, the paper strips were removed, and the supernatants were transferred to new tubes with 150 μl of PBS. Protein concentration was measured using a BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). 10 µg of protein were supplemented with 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate up to 70 µL., followed by protein reduction with 10 µL of 100 mM dithiothreitol (in 50 mM AmBic at 56°C for 30 minutes) and alkylation was performed by adding 20 µL of 100 mM iodoacetamide (in 50 mM AmBic at room temperature for 30 minutes). For protein digestion, trypsin was added to the samples (1:30 trypsin:protein) and incubated for 16 hours at 37°C. The digestion was halted with formic acid. Then, samples were cleaned on a C18 Hypersep plate (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) with 5-7 µL bed volume, dried using a vacuum concentrator (Eppendorf) and resuspended in 10 µL of 0.1% FA and 2% acetonitrile for subsequent analysis by HPRLC-MS/MS. Each GCF simple were proccesed for peptide separation using a 50 cm EASY-Spray C18 column connected to a high-performance liquid chromatography system, Ultimate 3000 nano-UPLC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific). A 90-minute linear gradient from 4% to 26% ACN in 0.1% formic acid was used at a flow rate of 300 nL/minute. Mass spectrometry was conducted using an Orbitrap Q Exactive HF instrument (Thermo Fisher Scientific) in data-dependent acquisition mode, with a mass range of 375–1500 m/z for full spectra. Blank runs were added after each analysis of biological replicates to minimize the carry over.
dataProcessingProtocol: The raw data files were loaded in Proteome Discoverer v2.4 software (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and searched against a human protein database using the Mascot Server 2.5.1 search engine (Matrix Science). As search parameters, a tolerance of 10 ppm were considered for precursor ions (MS search) and 0.02 Da for the HCD fragment ions (MS/MS search), with a maximum of 2 missed cleavage. Dynamic modifications of oxidation on methionine, deamidation of asparagine and glutamine and acetylation of N-termini were set. A maximum of 1% of false discovery rate (FDR) was set for both protein and peptide identification. For quantification, both unique and razor peptides were requested.
